title: Water between the bars
sub: Trapping Rain Water: three solutions and the proof of why we move the lower side
cards/0/title: The problem and the water-over-one-bar formula
cards/0/body:
Trapping Rain Water (LeetCode #42, hard). The array h holds the heights of bars of width 1. How much water is trapped after the rain? n ≤ 2·10⁴, 0 ≤ h ≤ 10⁵. Example: [0,1,0,2,1,0,1,3,2,1,2,1] → 6.

Do not think about whole “puddles” — count the water over each bar separately. The water over i rises to the lower of two “walls”: the highest bar on the left and the highest bar on the right.

water[i] = min(maxLeft[i], maxRight[i]) − h[i], where maxLeft[i] is the maximum of h[0..i] and maxRight[i] is the maximum of h[i..n − 1]. The bar itself is part of both maxima, so the difference is never negative: the highest bar holds no water.

Signals: the answer is a sum of per-position contributions, and each contribution depends on the maximum to the left and to the right. That invites prefix maxima — and two pointers, if memory must be O(1).
cards/1/q: h = [2, 0, 4, 1, 3]. How much water is over the bar at index 3 (height 1)?
cards/1/explain: The maximum to its left (itself included) is 4, to its right 3. The lower wall holds: min(4, 3) − 1 = 2. The array holds 4 in total: another 2 over index 1.
cards/1/wrong/1: That is 4 − 1: it takes the left wall, but the water spills over the lower one — the right wall of height 3.
cards/1/wrong/2: The bar’s neighbors (4 and 3) are higher than its 1 — there is water. What matters is not the neighbors but the maxima on each side.
cards/2/title: The naive solution: find the walls for every bar
cards/2/body:
Straight from the formula: for each i, scan left and right to find the maxima. That is O(n) per bar and O(n²) overall; O(1) memory. For n = 2·10⁴ it is about n · n = 4·10⁸ steps — several seconds at 10⁸ operations per second, while the limit is usually 1–2 seconds.

What work am I repeating? The left maximum for i + 1 is the maximum for i plus one more bar. Yet we recompute it from scratch every time. Same on the right.
cards/3/body:
Precompute all the maxima. A left pass: maxLeft[i] = max(maxLeft[i − 1], h[i]). A right pass: maxRight[i] = max(maxRight[i + 1], h[i]). A third pass adds up the water by the formula. Time O(n), memory O(n) — two arrays.

It is the same “remember the past instead of recomputing” as prefix sums from the hash map unit, just with max instead of +. An interviewer will accept this solution; the next question is “and with O(1) memory?”.
cards/4/title: Solution 2: two pointers, and why we move the lower side
cards/4/body:
For the water over a bar you do not need both maxima, only the smaller of the two. Pointers l and r walk toward each other from the ends; lmax is the maximum of what has been passed on the left, rmax on the right.

Rule: if h[l] < h[r], process l: lmax = max(lmax, h[l]), water lmax − h[l], l++. Otherwise do the same on the right with rmax.

Why the true right maximum is not needed. The left pointer only moves off the lower bar: every bar passed on the left was, at its moment, lower than h[r] for some r not to the left of the current one. So lmax is no greater than the maximum to the right of l, and neither is h[l] < h[r]. The lower of the two walls over l is the left one, max(lmax, h[l]), however high the right side is. Meanwhile rmax may still be 0: nothing on the right was passed yet, but h[r] already guarantees a wall at least that high.

Invariant: the water over every bar outside [l, r] is counted correctly, and the lower of h[l], h[r] is bounded by its own side. On a tie either side works. O(n) time, O(1) memory.
cards/5/q: h = [5, 1, 2, 9]. Step one: 5 < 9, lmax = 5, l = 1. Step two: h[1] = 1 < h[3] = 9, rmax is still 0, and the code adds 5 − 1 = 4. Why is that correct?
cards/5/options/0: There is guaranteed to be a wall of at least 9 on the right, and 5 on the left — the left side holds the water over l
cards/5/options/1: The right pointer has not moved yet, so water on the right is not counted
cards/5/options/2: It is a bug: it should be min(lmax, rmax) − h[l] = 0
cards/5/explain: rmax is the maximum of the bars passed on the right only, not of all of them. The true maximum to the right of l is at least h[r] = 9, the left one is 5. The lower wall holds: 5 − 1 = 4. The total for this array is 7: another 3 over the 2.
cards/5/wrong/1: The water over l depends on both walls; the right one is simply proven higher than the left, so its exact value is not needed.
cards/5/wrong/2: rmax = 0 is incomplete knowledge, not a wall of height 0. The formula with min(lmax, rmax) would give 0 and lose the water.
cards/6/explain: Process the lower side: h[l] < h[r] means the left one. lmax already includes h[l], so lmax − h[l] is never negative. The right side is symmetric: rmax − h[r]. Math.Min(lmax, rmax) would lose water while rmax is still small, and h[r] − h[l] takes the right wall as the water level.
cards/7/task: Step through the trace on [0, 1, 0, 2, 1, 0, 1, 3, 2, 1, 2, 1]. The rig stops twice: decide which side the code processes and how much water it records.
cards/7/goal/asks/0/options/0/label: Processes R: rmax = 2, water 0, R moves
cards/7/goal/asks/0/options/1/label: Processes L: lmax = 2, water 0, L moves
cards/7/goal/asks/0/q: L moved to index 3 (height 2), R is at index 10 (height 2). The heights are equal. What does the code do?
cards/7/goal/asks/0/explain: The condition h[l] < h[r] is strict: 2 < 2 is false, so the code goes to else and processes the right side. On a tie either side works: the wall on the other side is at least as high, and the proof holds for both.
cards/7/goal/asks/1/q: L = 5 (height 0), R = 7 (height 3), lmax = 2, rmax = 2. How much water does the code record over bar 5?
cards/7/goal/asks/1/explain: h[5] = 0 < h[R] = 3 — the left side is processed. The wall on the right is at least 3, on the left it is 2, and the lower one holds: 2 − 0 = 2. h[R] = 3 is only a guarantee that the right wall is no lower than lmax, not the water level.
cards/8/title: Solution 3: a monotonic stack — water in layers
cards/8/body:
A third view counts water not per bar but in horizontal layers. Keep a stack of indices whose heights do not increase from bottom to top. When h[i] is higher than the top, the top bottom has found its right wall. Pop it; the new top left is the left wall. The layer between them has width i − left − 1 and height min(h[left], h[i]) − h[bottom]. Repeat while h[i] is higher than the top, then push i.

The nested while does not make it quadratic: every index is pushed and popped once, at most 2n stack operations in total. Time O(n), O(n) memory for the stack. This is the “nearest greater to the left and right” template; the stacks unit is devoted to monotonic stacks.

The solution is useful when data arrives one value at a time, left to right: two pointers need the whole array at once, while the stack needs only the past.
cards/9/q: On [3, 0, 5] this code returns 7 instead of 3. Tap the line with the bug.
cards/9/explain: A copy-paste from the right branch: lmax takes h[r] instead of h[l]. On the first step lmax = 5, so 5 − 3 = 2 water appears over the 3 and 5 over the 0. But h[r] is only a guarantee that the right wall is no lower; the water level over l is set by the maximum passed on the left. It should be lmax = Math.Max(lmax, h[l]).
cards/10/q: What is true about the three solutions? Select all.
cards/10/options/0: Prefix maxima: O(n) time and O(n) memory
cards/10/options/1: Two pointers need the whole array at once, while the stack walks left to right and only looks at the past
cards/10/options/2: In the two-pointer solution rmax always equals the true maximum to the right of l
cards/10/options/3: When h[l] == h[r], either side can be processed
cards/10/options/4: The monotonic stack is O(n²) in the worst case because of the nested while
cards/10/explain: Prefixes are two arrays of size n. Two pointers start from the right end, the stack does not. rmax is the maximum of what has been passed on the right only and can be smaller than the true one; the whole proof is that it is not needed. On a tie the wall on the other side is no lower — either side works. The stack is O(n): every index is pushed and popped once.
cards/11/q: You are solving Trapping Rain Water out loud. Put the steps in order.
cards/11/items/0: Clarify: n, the range of heights, whether the array can be empty
cards/11/items/1: The formula: water over i = min(max on the left, max on the right) − h[i]
cards/11/items/2: Naively: find the walls for every i — O(n²)
cards/11/items/3: Remove the repetition: maxLeft and maxRight arrays — O(n) time and memory
cards/11/items/4: Two pointers: process the lower side, its own side sets the level — O(1) memory
cards/11/items/6: Complexity and edge cases: n < 3, a monotonic array, a flat plateau
cards/11/explain: The single-bar formula is the key to all three solutions, so it comes right after clarifying. Then the ladder: O(n²) → O(n) with memory → O(n) without, and at every step — which repeated work was removed.
cards/12/title: Where this shows up in games, and what comes next
cards/12/body:
The 2D version (Trapping Rain Water II, #407): a height map with water in the pits. Pointers do not work there — the “lower side” is now the whole boundary of the region. The solution is a heap over the boundary: pop the lowest boundary cell, its unvisited neighbors fill up to its level and become boundary themselves. It is a Dijkstra-style traversal, O(wh · log(wh)); heaps and pathfinding come in later units.

In a game: filling lakes on procedural terrain, puddles on a height map, the water level in a tile simulator. A profile along one line is exactly problem #42.

Overflow: the water is less than n · max h = 2·10⁴ · 10⁵ = 2·10⁹ — that still fits in an int (2,147,483,647), but barely. With other constraints, accumulate in a long.
cards/12/deep:
Two pointers as a merge of prefixes. Solution 2 is solution 1 where, at any moment, only the array whose maximum is smaller is read. The left prefix only grows to the right, the right suffix only to the left, and the pointers simply walk them toward each other; nothing extra is stored.

Formally. Suppose at some step h[l] < h[r]. Every bar k < l was passed at a step where h[k] < h[r_k] and r_k ≥ r > l, so lmax < max(h[l + 1..n − 1]), and h[l] < h[r] too. Hence min(maxLeft[l], maxRight[l]) = max(lmax, h[l]). The right branch is symmetric with a non-strict inequality.

Performance. Prefix arrays are three linear passes: the CPU predicts such access well, and Burst can vectorize a pass with max. Two pointers branch on every step. For n = 2·10⁴ all three solutions take tens of microseconds; argue about memory and clarity, not speed.

Allocations. new Stack<int>() and the arrays are garbage if the function runs every frame. In Unity keep the stack in a field and call Clear(), or for a small n use Span<int> st = stackalloc int[n] with a manual top (the thread stack is limited, usually 1 MB — not for large n).
cards/13/q: Match each solution with its cost.
cards/13/pairs/0/0: Scanning for walls for every i
cards/13/pairs/3/1: O(n), one left-to-right pass, stack up to n
cards/13/pairs/4/1: Heap over the boundary, O(wh · log(wh))
